doc.title: Don Wolff interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 13, 1996

title: Critique of this year's Sarasota festival and its sound
summary: Wolff was disappointed by the first night and the sound problems, and they discuss who selects musicians.

story.theme_name: Still working: current gigs, upcoming projects and plans
story.community_name: What's next: upcoming tours, records and plans

blocks.x: Boy he was never at a loss for a line, was he? Well what do you think of this particular festival here at Sarasota?

Well I love the festival. I’ve been disappointed with this year’s edition, certainly not with the number of musicians and the wealth of their abilities, but I didn’t think the first night clicked. I’m a Jazz at the Phil fan, it’s one of my favorites. To be told that I’m going to get a chance to listen to jam session and then a ballad medley with all of these great artists, I would have expected a lot more. I just didn’t think it gelled. It didn’t come together for some reason. I’m not sure I know why, but I’ve been thinking about it ever since Wednesday night, and it just didn’t come together. So I was disappointed in that. Last night I was very disappointed in the sound, which I think adversely affected The Statesmen, who I know to be a great group, and to see Benny Waters, 93 years young playing the horn better than most people can play at the age of 23, was just a thrill. But to have it all destroyed by the lack of the microphones being on or by the sound being too loud, was very discouraging. So last night I felt was a disappointing evening. The night in between those two nights I think was a great night, and I think the Count Basie Band will bring us all what we expect.

I’m thinking of wearing neck brace, because I know they’re going to take my head off when they hit that first chord, after hearing them this afternoon. You know I think someone could make a good living being a jazz sound man. I think that we have, I don’t know if we’ve demanded over the years, to make things louder, but it seems they don’t allow the musicians to set anything themselves somehow.

Well I thought part of the problems last night was one of the musicians setting his own volume on his amp and that was the violin and he set it much, much too loud and I think his own age, in the 80s, almost 90, and his inability to hear like other people hear, may have affected it. I’m not sure but there’s no excuse for an organization like this one to not have good sound. And I don’t want to blame that on the musicians, I blame that on the professionals.
Well I give these people credit. It’s a big production. And sometimes pairing musicians can be a real dicey game, you know?

Oh, very difficult, in fact that’s one of the reasons the president of the Jazz Club here, who is a classmate of mine by the way and a good friend of mine, and one of the reasons I come here is because of him, but it’s one of the main reasons he started delegating that to other people is that he just got so much grief by who he picked and who he didn’t pick, that he turned it over to professionals like he did this year. But it does lose a little bit of the personal touch. I mean I’ve always liked at least in my own mind, to orchestrate my own festival. Who would I have if it were me?
Well I think you should put on a festival.
